title: KTO: Model Alignment as Prospect Theoretic Optimization

pages.title: Aligning models with thumbs-up / thumbs-down
pages.subtitle: Why pairwise preferences are a luxury you usually can't afford

blocks.html: The problem. To make a language model behave the way people want (helpful, harmless, on-topic), the standard recipe is RLHF or its direct cousin DPO. Both need preference pairs: for the same prompt, a human must say output A is better than output B. That data is expensive, slow, and often unnatural to collect — most real feedback in the wild is not a comparison at all.

The everyday analogy. Think about how feedback actually arrives in a product. A user clicks the thumbs-up on a chatbot reply, or the thumbs-down. A support agent marks a drafted email as send it or scrap it. Nobody hands you two replies and asks which is better — they hand you one reply and a single binary verdict. KTO is built to learn directly from exactly this signal: a prompt, an output, and one bit saying desirable or undesirable.

The key idea in one sentence. The authors notice that DPO's loss already secretly contains a function from prospect theory — the Nobel-winning model of how humans value gains and losses, by Kahneman and Tversky. They make this connection explicit, name the whole family HALOs (Human-Aware Losses), and then design a new member, KTO (Kahneman-Tversky Optimization), whose loss directly maximizes the utility of an output rather than the log-likelihood of a preferred output over a dispreferred one.

Kahneman & Tversky's prospect theory tells us that humans perceive random variables in a biased but well-defined manner; for example, relative to some reference point, humans are more sensitive to losses than gains, a property called loss aversion.

The headline result. Despite using a strictly weaker signal (binary labels instead of pairs), KTO matches or beats DPO across model scales from 1B to 30B parameters. Even more striking: KTO can learn from data where the desirable and undesirable examples are extremely imbalanced (up to a 1-to-10 ratio), and on some setups, skipping supervised fine-tuning and running KTO alone still works — something DPO cannot do.

Why it mattered. Pairwise data is the bottleneck in alignment. By unlocking the much larger pool of binary feedback — and feedback that is naturally generated by users every day — KTO made alignment cheaper and more practical. It was quickly adopted into open-source alignment libraries (TRL, Axolotl) and sits in the lineage that runs from RLHF (Christiano, Ouyang) through DPO (Rafailov et al., 2023) to the simpler, data-efficient methods that followed.

pages.title: From RLHF's reward maximization to DPO's closed-form loss
pages.subtitle: What KTO is reacting against

blocks.html: What this page answers. KTO is best understood as a redesign of DPO, which is itself a shortcut around RLHF. So before the new idea, we need the two methods it replaces — and, crucially, the exact reward expression that DPO leaves behind, because KTO reuses it.

RLHF in three steps. (1) Collect preference pairs and fit a reward model $r$ that scores outputs. (2) Use reinforcement learning (PPO) to push the policy $\pi_\theta$ toward high-reward outputs, while a KL penalty keeps it from drifting too far from the supervised-fine-tuned reference model $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. The RL objective is:

blocks.tex: \max_{\pi_\theta}\; \mathbb{E}_{x\sim D,\, y\sim \pi_\theta(\cdot\mid x)}\big[\, r(x,y)\,\big] \;-\; \beta\, \mathrm{KL}\!\left(\pi_\theta(y\mid x)\,\|\,\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)\right)

blocks.html: Reading it term by term: $x$ is a prompt drawn from dataset $D$; $y$ is an output the policy $\pi_\theta$ samples; $r(x,y)\in\mathbb{R}$ is the learned reward; $\pi_{\text{ref}}$ is the frozen starting model; $\mathrm{KL}(\cdot\|\cdot)$ measures how far the policy has moved from it; and $\beta>0$ is the knob trading off reward against staying close to $\pi_{\text{ref}}$. Large $\beta$ = stay cautious; small $\beta$ = chase reward aggressively.

DPO's shortcut. Rafailov et al. (2023) showed the RL objective above has a closed-form optimum, which can be inverted to express the implied reward purely in terms of the policy and reference — no separate reward model, no RL loop. The implied reward is:

Here $\pi_\theta(y\mid x)$ is the probability the trained model assigns to output $y$, and $\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)$ the reference's probability; their log-ratio, scaled by $\beta$, is the reward. Intuitively: an output is rewarded to the extent the aligned model has come to favor it more than the original model did. This single expression is the engine KTO inherits — KTO keeps this $r_\theta$ and only changes the loss wrapped around it.

Why this framing matters. By turning reward into a log-ratio of probabilities, DPO converts alignment into a plain supervised loss over pairs. But it still needs pairs: the DPO loss compares a chosen $y_w$ against a rejected $y_l$. KTO's whole contribution is removing that pairwise requirement while keeping the elegant log-ratio reward.

pages.title: Prospect theory: how humans really value gains and losses
pages.subtitle: The psychology KTO is built on

blocks.html: What this page answers. KTO's loss is not pulled from thin air — it is a direct translation of how Kahneman and Tversky modeled human decision-making. To understand the loss, you first need the value function from prospect theory.

The intuition. A purely rational agent values money linearly: $+\$100$ is exactly as good as $-\$100$ is bad. Humans don't work that way. We feel losses more sharply than equivalent gains (loss aversion), we measure everything relative to a reference point rather than in absolute terms, and our sensitivity to change flattens out as the amounts get larger (diminishing sensitivity).

A concrete example. Offered a coin flip that wins you $\$100$ on heads and loses $\$100$ on tails — a fair, zero-expected-value bet — most people decline. Losing $\$100$ stings more than gaining $\$100$ pleases. Tversky and Kahneman estimated the pain of a loss is roughly 2x the pleasure of the same-sized gain. That asymmetry is the loss-aversion coefficient $\lambda$.
The Kahneman-Tversky value function. Their fitted model of human utility, for an outcome $z$ relative to reference point $z_0$, is:

blocks.tex: v(z,z_0) \;=\; \begin{cases} (z - z_0)^{\alpha} & \text{if } z \geq z_0 \\[4pt] -\lambda\,(z_0 - z)^{\alpha} & \text{if } z < z_0 \end{cases}

blocks.html: Term by term: $z$ is the realized outcome (e.g. dollars, or here a reward); $z_0$ is the reference point separating gains from losses; the exponent $\alpha\approx 0.88$ controls diminishing sensitivity (the curve bends, so the 10th dollar matters less than the 1st); and $\lambda\approx 2.25$ is the loss-aversion coefficient that makes the losing branch steeper than the winning branch. The function is concave for gains and convex for losses — an S-shape pinned at $z_0$.

Why this is the right lens for alignment. The authors argue that any sensible alignment loss is implicitly modeling a human who perceives a reward, relative to some baseline, in this biased way. Making that model explicit lets you design losses on purpose instead of by accident — and lets you see that DPO is already one such loss in disguise.

pages.title: HALOs: Human-Aware Losses as a unifying family
pages.subtitle: DPO and PPO as special cases of one template

blocks.html: What this page answers. Having the prospect-theory value function in hand, the authors define a general template — a HALO (Human-Aware Loss) — and show that DPO and the RLHF/PPO objective both fall out of it as special cases. This is the conceptual heart of the paper: alignment losses are value functions over an implied reward.

The template. A loss is a HALO if it can be written so that the model's per-example contribution passes a learned reward $r_\theta(x,y)$, measured relative to a reference point $\mathbb{E}[r_\theta]$, through a value function $v$ shaped like the prospect-theory one — concave in gains, possibly steeper in losses:

Reading it term by term: $r_\theta(x,y)$ is the implied reward (the same $\beta\log$ ratio from DPO); the expectation $\mathbb{E}_{x',y'}[r_\theta(x',y')]$ is the reference point $z_0$ — the average reward the model assigns, i.e. the baseline gains and losses are measured against; $v$ is a non-decreasing, concave-in-the-gains value function; and $t\in\{+1,-1\}$ (or a weight) marks whether this example should be pushed up or down. A loss built from such $f$ across the dataset is a HALO.

DPO is a HALO. Plug in the logistic function $\sigma$ as the value function and use the difference of two outputs' rewards as the argument, and you recover DPO exactly. The reference point in DPO is implicitly the rejected output's reward — gains are measured against the dispreferred sample. PPO/RLHF is also a HALO, with its own (less loss-averse) implied value function.
We call this family of loss functions human-aware losses (HALOs)... we find that the HALOs we consider — DPO and our proposed KTO — outperform their non-HALO counterparts.

Why the unification pays off. Once you see alignment losses as value functions over a reference-relative reward, two design freedoms open up. First, you can choose the value function deliberately — and pick one with real loss aversion. Second, and the decisive one, the reference point need not be a paired counter-example. It can be a dataset-level baseline, which is what frees KTO from needing pairs at all.

pages.title: The KTO loss: maximizing utility from a single binary label
pages.subtitle: One output, one bit, no pairs

blocks.html: What this page answers. This is the core construction. Given a prompt $x$, an output $y$, and a single label saying whether $y$ is desirable or undesirable, how do we build a HALO loss that needs no paired counter-example? KTO's answer: use a global reference point that any single example can be compared against.

The reference point. KTO sets the reference $z_0$ to be the model's average implied reward — estimated as the KL divergence between the policy and reference over the prompt distribution. Concretely, the baseline term is

Here $z_0$ is a single scalar computed by averaging $\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}$ over outputs $y'$ sampled for prompts in the batch. It is the "typical" amount the model has moved from the reference — the dividing line above which an output counts as a gain and below which it counts as a loss. Crucially this depends only on the prompt, not on any paired competitor, which is why a lone labeled example suffices.
The per-example value. For a desirable output we want its reward to sit above the reference; for an undesirable one, below. KTO uses the logistic $\sigma$ as its concave value function and writes:

blocks.tex: v(x,y) \;=\; \begin{cases} \lambda_D\,\sigma\!\big(\beta\,(\, r_\theta(x,y) - z_0\,)\big) & \text{if } y \sim y_{\text{desirable}} \\[6pt] \lambda_U\,\sigma\!\big(\beta\,(\, z_0 - r_\theta(x,y)\,)\big) & \text{if } y \sim y_{\text{undesirable}} \end{cases}

blocks.html: Term by term: $r_\theta(x,y)=\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta(y\mid x)}{\pi_{\text{ref}}(y\mid x)}$ is the inherited DPO reward; $z_0$ is the global reference above; $\sigma$ is the logistic squashing function giving an S-shaped, saturating value; $\beta$ controls how steep the squash is. For a desirable $y$ the argument is $(r_\theta - z_0)$, so the value rises as the reward beats the baseline; for an undesirable $y$ it is flipped to $(z_0 - r_\theta)$, so the value rises as the reward falls below baseline. $\lambda_D,\lambda_U>0$ are the desirable/undesirable weights — the loss-aversion knobs.

The loss to minimize. KTO maximizes total value, i.e. minimizes $\lambda_y - v(x,y)$ averaged over the data, where $\lambda_y$ is $\lambda_D$ or $\lambda_U$ depending on the label. Pushing this down does the intuitive thing: it raises $\pi_\theta$'s probability on outputs marked good (lifting their reward above $z_0$) and lowers it on outputs marked bad (pushing their reward below $z_0$) — gradient by gradient, with the logistic saturating so the model doesn't over-commit to any single example.

pages.title: Loss aversion as a class-imbalance knob
pages.subtitle: Why λ_D and λ_U are the secret weapon

blocks.html: What this page answers. Two parameters, $\lambda_D$ and $\lambda_U$, weight the desirable and undesirable terms. They look like minor hyperparameters but they are where prospect-theoretic loss aversion meets a very practical problem: real binary-feedback datasets are rarely balanced.

The intuition. Recall loss aversion: humans weight a loss about 2x a gain. KTO bakes the same asymmetry in by choosing $\lambda_U$ and $\lambda_D$. But the same knobs also rebalance the data. If you have ten times as many thumbs-up examples as thumbs-down, the undesirable signal would be drowned out — unless you up-weight each undesirable example to compensate.
The recommended rule. The authors suggest keeping the effective contribution of each class roughly balanced. If $n_D$ desirable and $n_U$ undesirable examples are in a batch, set the weights so that

Reading it: $\lambda_D n_D$ is the total pull from desirable examples, $\lambda_U n_U$ the total pull from undesirable ones; their ratio is kept near 1 (with a mild lean, up to $4/3$, toward the desirable side reflecting loss aversion on the model's side). In practice you fix one weight to 1 and solve for the other from your class counts. This single rule is what lets KTO ingest wildly imbalanced feedback streams.

The payoff (real numbers). The authors show KTO stays strong even at a 1:10 imbalance between desirable and undesirable data — and that with this balancing, you can discard up to 90% of the desirable examples (keeping the rarer class) and still beat DPO, as long as the weights are adjusted. No comparable knob exists in DPO, which is locked into one-good-one-bad pairs by construction.

Why it works. Because KTO's reference point is global rather than a paired counter-example, each example contributes an independent gradient. That independence is exactly what makes per-class re-weighting meaningful — you can dial the importance of an entire class without having to find it a partner. The trade-off: you now have two hyperparameters to tune, but the simple $[1, 4/3]$ heuristic removes most of the search.

pages.title: KTO matches or beats DPO from 1B to 30B
pages.subtitle: The headline experiments

blocks.html: What this page answers. The big claim is that a method using a weaker signal (binary labels) can match one using a stronger signal (preference pairs). Does that hold up across model sizes and benchmarks? The authors test on the Pythia (1.4B, 2.8B, 6.9B) and Llama (7B, 13B, 30B) families.

The setup. Even when genuine preference pairs are available, KTO can use them by simply splitting each pair into two binary examples: the chosen output becomes a desirable example, the rejected output an undesirable one. This makes a clean head-to-head possible — same underlying data, DPO sees it as pairs, KTO sees it as independent labels. Win rates are judged by GPT-4 on held-out prompts.
KTO matches or exceeds DPO performance at scales from 1B to 30B parameters... despite the fact that it does not need paired preference data and can even handle extreme data imbalances.

The MMLU / benchmark picture. Beyond GPT-4 win rates, the aligned models are checked on standard benchmarks (MMLU, GSM8K, HumanEval, BBH). KTO-aligned models hold or improve these scores while becoming more helpful — alignment does not come at the cost of raw capability. At 13B and 30B, KTO-aligned models post some of the best aggregate scores in the comparison.

Why this is surprising. Information-theoretically, a binary label carries less than a pairwise comparison (a pair implicitly contains two labels plus their ordering). That KTO ties or wins anyway suggests the pairwise format was never the source of DPO's power — the value-function shape and the reference point were. KTO keeps those and drops the costly part.

pages.title: KTO can skip SFT and survive on imbalanced data
pages.subtitle: Where KTO does things DPO simply cannot

blocks.html: What this page answers. Matching DPO is impressive, but the more important results are the things KTO can do that DPO cannot — because those are the situations real practitioners face.

Result 1: KTO alone, no SFT. The usual pipeline is SFT then preference optimization. The authors find that for sufficiently large models (e.g. Llama-13B/30B), running KTO directly on the pretrained model, with no supervised fine-tuning stage, already produces a well-aligned model. DPO without a preceding SFT stage degrades badly — its loss assumes the model already places reasonable mass on the chosen outputs, which a raw pretrained model does not.

Result 2: extreme imbalance. Using the $\lambda_D,\lambda_U$ balancing rule, KTO trains successfully even when one class is up to 10x rarer than the other. The authors deliberately throw away large fractions of the majority class and show performance is retained. This mirrors production reality, where thumbs-down is far rarer than thumbs-up.

Result 3: noisy, intransitive feedback. Because KTO scores each output on an absolute desirable/undesirable basis rather than forcing a consistent ordering, it is more robust when human feedback is noisy or intransitive (A>B, B>C, but C>A) — situations that violate the consistency a pairwise model assumes.

Theoretically, KTO is also easier to use in the real world... it does not require preferences, only a binary signal of whether an output is desirable or undesirable for a given input, which is far more abundant and cheaper to collect.

Why it works. All three abilities trace back to one design choice: the global, KL-based reference point instead of a paired counter-example. It decouples examples (enabling re-weighting and imbalance handling), it gives an absolute target the loss can pull toward even from a raw model (enabling SFT-free training), and it avoids assuming a globally consistent preference order (enabling robustness to intransitivity).

The lasting idea. KTO's deepest contribution is conceptual: it reframes alignment losses as value functions over a reference-relative reward (the HALO view), making explicit a connection to prospect theory that was hiding inside DPO. Once you see the family, designing a new member that needs only binary labels is natural — and that member turned out to match the pairwise state of the art.

The practical unlock. Binary feedback is everywhere and nearly free: every thumbs-up/down, every accept/reject, every flagged message is a label. By learning from it directly, KTO removed the preference-pair bottleneck that made RLHF and DPO expensive to apply. Teams could now align on the feedback their product already collects.

items: Cheaper data: binary signals replace costly, slow pairwise annotation — and arise organically from real users.
Imbalance-robust: the $\lambda_D/\lambda_U$ rule handles class ratios up to 1:10, matching messy production feedback.
SFT-optional: for large models, KTO can align a pretrained model with no supervised fine-tuning stage, which DPO cannot.
Drop-in: KTO reuses DPO's implied reward $\beta\log\frac{\pi_\theta}{\pi_{\text{ref}}}$, so it slots into existing DPO codepaths with minimal change.

blocks.html: Where it sits in the lineage. The path runs from RLHF (Christiano et al. 2017; Ouyang et al. / InstructGPT 2022) — reward model plus PPO — to DPO (Rafailov et al. 2023), which removed the RL loop, to KTO, which removed the pairwise data requirement. KTO sits alongside other DPO successors (IPO, SLiC, ORPO) as part of the 2023–2024 wave simplifying alignment, and it is the one that re-grounded the whole enterprise in human decision psychology.

Adoption. KTO was integrated into mainstream open-source alignment tooling — Hugging Face's TRL ships a KTOTrainer, and frameworks like Axolotl expose it as a first-class objective — so practitioners can align on thumbs-up/down data with a few config lines. Its prospect-theory framing also opened a small research thread on deliberately shaping the value function for alignment, rather than inheriting one by accident.
